purpose: Lidocaine is used to numb a specific area of your body so you don't feel pain during procedures, injections, or minor surgeries. It can also be applied to the skin or mucous membranes to relieve pain, itching, or irritation. In certain situations, it is given through an IV to treat an irregular heartbeat.
how_it_works: Lidocaine works by temporarily blocking the nerve signals in the area where it is applied or injected. Think of it like hitting a pause button on the nerves that send pain messages to your brain. This numbing effect wears off on its own after a few hours once the medication clears from that area.
common_side_effects: At the site where it is used, you might notice temporary numbness, tingling, redness, or mild irritation. If used in larger amounts or given by IV, some people feel dizzy, drowsy, or have a mild headache. These effects are usually short-lived.
warnings: Tell your doctor if you have heart problems, liver disease, or are allergic to any anesthetics. Using too much lidocaine, especially on large areas of broken or irritated skin, can cause serious side effects like seizures, irregular heartbeat, or difficulty breathing. Never use more than your doctor or the label directs, and keep it away from children.
typical_dosing: Dosing depends on how lidocaine is being used. For numbing skin creams or gels, a thin layer is usually applied to the affected area 1 to 4 times a day as needed. For injections or IV use, your doctor or nurse will calculate the right dose based on your weight and the procedure. Always follow your healthcare provider's exact instructions.
